column3: Exact parallel: every sign fails to produce belief until the painful punishment is seen.
Adds sudden, unperceived punishment as the collapse of false security.
Contrasts belief and turning away, with Fire as the consequence of refusal.
Restates refusal to believe and frames it as an inherited pattern.
The sound heart supplies a limited contrast to the criminals' unreceptive inner state.
Exact parallel links closed hearts, delayed belief, and seeing painful punishment.
Makes the painful punishment an experienced reality rather than a warning alone.
The immediate continuation specifies that the event comes suddenly while they are unaware.
Shows belief as the alternative that removes any purpose for punishment.
Joins disbelief in the Hereafter to punishment and far error.
The local sequence adds their provocative demand to hasten the punishment.
Offers only a distant contrast between seeing and the heart's truthful reception.
Directly identifies the punishment as painful, without the focus's delayed-belief condition.
Depicts a painful punishment overtaking people as an encompassing event.
Reiterates punishment and warning but adds little after the nearer parallels.
Treats a remaining sign as warning for those who fear painful punishment.
The revelation's descent supplies the message entering before the criminals refuse belief.
Turning away from the reminder leads into an arduous punishment.
Provides the positive counterpart: prior recipients believe in this revelation.
The next local response asks for delay after the sudden arrival described in the passage.
States that the Lord's punishment is not safely assumed away.
The opponents dismiss a messenger and defer judgment, only loosely matching refusal.
Pairs the fixed divine word with persistent nonbelief, directly clarifying the focus's condition.
Seeing one's smallest evil deed is only a broad accountability parallel.
Defines genuine belief as accepting judgment inwardly as well as outwardly.
The revelation placed on the messenger's heart establishes the warning refused in the focus.
The local deniers explicitly assert that they will not be punished.
Names disbelief but its legal setting does not explain the focus's late belief.
Begins the local question whether years of enjoyment alter the eventual outcome.
Associates futile disputation with severe punishment, without the seeing threshold.
Those who see every sign still do not believe, closely defining resistant perception.
The immediately preceding verse locates the message within the hearts of criminals.
Its statement of scant belief in the revelation supports the passage's refusal motif.
Seeing punishment brings concealed regret and just judgment, showing the late consequence.
Completes the local sequence: what they were promised finally comes to them.
Faith and righteous action yield freedom from fear and grief, a clear outcome contrast.
Visible signs are said to benefit believers, but the scene is otherwise remote.
States that prior enjoyment proves useless once the promised event has arrived.
Punishment of disbelievers is present, but the military setting adds little.
Calls for seeing signs that support belief, in a specific provision setting.
Rejecting recited signs culminates in announcement of painful punishment.
Safety from hunger and fear does not clarify refusal until punishment is seen.
Lesser punishment is experienced as a chance to return before the greater one.
The local rationale says destroyed towns had already received warners.
The natural sign of rain and greening adds no focused link.
Disbelief in the Hereafter is shown as a present departure from the straight path.
The sound-heart channel supplies only an indirect positive contrast.
Its description of a protected environment does not bear on the focus.
Offers separation rather than compelled belief when a messenger is rejected.
The local statement makes the warning a reminder and denies injustice in the outcome.
Shares punishment among those jointly implicated in the error.
Sets turning away against the greatest punishment.
Their demand to hasten punishment is answered by the encompassing reality of Hell.
Distinguishes worldly punishment from a greater Hereafter punishment.
Under punishment they claim belief, directly illustrating belated profession.
A sound heart offers a limited contrast to the criminal hearts in the focus.
Asks what message could still elicit belief after this one is refused.
The lunar cycle has no material connection to the focus.
Calls those already believing to trust, rather than explaining refusal.
Seeing a great sign is only a broad contrast to seeing punishment.
Links refusal to believe Allah's signs with lack of guidance and painful punishment.
The believers' prayer for protection does not add to the focus.
Repeats the punishment-and-warning formula without a new element.
Prepares painful punishment for those who disbelieve in the Hereafter.
Sudden arrival of the Hour leaves no effective later reminder.
Fear of the Lord's punishment is a general counterposture to the focus.
The rhetorical question isolates the basic failure to believe.
A messenger is rejected as merely human and falsely sent, extending the refusal pattern.
Commands the disbelievers to taste the punishment of the Fire.
Visible security is met with false belief and ingratitude, only loosely related.
The messengers' affirmation of their mission does not develop the punishment threshold.
A warning of painful punishment follows turning away, but in a distinct proclamation.
Contrasts believers in revelation with rejecters whose appointed meeting is the Fire.
The conflict around warning is relevant, but this response adds little to 26:201.
Offers salvation from painful punishment to believers in a broad exhortative setting.
Those in error see the promised punishment or Hour and only then know the truth.
Hastening punishment, its appointed term, and sudden unaware arrival closely reinforce the focus.
Divine hearing and seeing do not clarify human seeing of punishment.
Seeing punishment reveals Allah's total power too late for the wrongdoers.
The question about entry into Saqar adds only a narrow consequence frame.
Makes eternal punishment the consequence of conduct, after the meeting is denied.
Even seeing every sign does not yield belief for the arrogant, a close resistant-perception parallel.
Turning away alone is too general after stronger refusal cards.
A separate visionary event does not illuminate belief after punishment.
Observing a natural sign is directed to believers, only broadly contrasting the focus.
Future visibility of one's striving offers a general accountability parallel.
Shows that apparent belief can remain compromised by associationism.
Exchanging belief for disbelief is joined to painful punishment.
The fragment naming criminals adds no usable explanation by itself.
A human threat of painful punishment does not explain the divine consequence in the focus.
The image of raised dust has no material connection.
Lot's belief supplies a remote positive counterpart to rejection.
Those in the Fire seek even one day of relief, displaying the reality of punishment.
Hell is made visible to the one who sees, directly supporting visible consequence.
The question about human emission is unrelated to the focus.
The local refrain joins a manifest sign to the fact that most still do not believe.
The enduring burden on the Day of Resurrection is only a general consequence.
Foretells the unavoidable sight of Hell.
The believers' forgiveness and generous provision form a broad outcome contrast.
Pharaoh treats belief as unauthorized and answers it with threatened bodily punishment.
Even sworn promises to believe upon receiving a sign do not establish that signs will produce belief.
Hearts and sight are turned away because they did not believe at the first encounter with signs.
Even every extraordinary confirmation would not make them believe unless Allah willed.
Former peoples received clear proofs yet would not believe what they had previously denied.
Later communities likewise reject the clear proofs brought by their messengers.
Even ascent through an opened gate of heaven would be dismissed as impaired sight or enchantment.
The history of denied signs explains why signs are inseparable from the prospect of punishment.
Guidance comes, yet people withhold belief through an objection to the human messenger.
What prevents belief after guidance is the demand that earlier destruction or punishment arrive before them.
No destroyed town had believed before its punishment, posing the same challenge to later hearers.

One hears Allah's signs and then persists arrogantly, followed by announcement of painful punishment.
Seeing a sign leads to turning away and calling it persistent magic, a concentrated resistant-perception parallel.

Warning does not alter the settled disbelievers' refusal to believe.
The deaf, dumb, and blind response image portrays reception without understanding.

When signs are recited, the response reduces them to tales of former peoples.
Sealed hearts, hearing, and sight explain the heedlessness accompanying unbelief.

Opponents make belief conditional on escalating spectacular demands rather than received guidance.
Demanding angels or the vision of the Lord externalizes the threshold for accepting the message.
The demand for further signs is answered by locating signs with Allah and the messenger's role in clear warning.
Clear verses are rejected as a falsehood, and the revealed truth as manifest magic.
Seeing a sign leads to ridicule rather than assent.
Covered hearts and deaf ears are invoked to refuse the messenger's call while maintaining separation.

Clear verses are met by calling the manifest truth obvious magic.
Denial persists through following desire even after the sign is seen.
